questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What would substantiate a claim of contribution
questions.learningObjective: Explain what evidence would substantiate a claim of scholarly contribution
questions.stem: In a beekeeper's research log, Ano claims her two-year survey of hive temperatures contributed new knowledge about winter clustering. Explain what would substantiate that claim.

answer.exemplar: Substantiation requires evidence that the knowledge was not already available and that it was obtained systematically. Ano would need to show what earlier accounts of winter clustering did and did not record, identify the specific gap her survey fills, and provide the records, methods and analysis that make the finding checkable by others. A first-hand dataset alone shows work done, not contribution; the gap and the checkability turn effort into contribution.

questions.explanation: Contribution is a claim about what was added, not about effort spent. A dataset, a clear method and an explicit account of the gap earlier work left open are what make the claim checkable.
questions.hint: Ask what the earlier work had not already shown.

questions.explanation: A claim about the absence of work needs a search that could have found it and a record of where the search went. Two journals and one small shelf cannot support a claim about the whole literature.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A methods section contradicted by the appendix
questions.learningObjective: Explain the problem created when an appendix contradicts the methods
questions.stem: In a beekeeper's logbook, the methods section says observations were made every second day, while an appendix table shows entries for irregular intervals. Explain the problem this creates.

answer.exemplar: The two parts of the paper now tell the reader different stories about the same evidence. The methods section describes a regular schedule, and the appendix reveals that the record contains gaps and clusters instead. A reader who trusts the methods will interpret the irregular entries as meaningful variation in the hive, when they may simply be days nobody looked. The claim built on that interpretation therefore rests on a description the evidence contradicts.

questions.explanation: The methods section tells the reader how to interpret the data, and the appendix shows the data do not fit that description. The conflict leaves the reader unsure which account of the study to believe.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader will assume from each part.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A methods section contradicted by the appendix
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a contradiction with the methods distorts the reading of data
questions.stem: A logbook study states in its methods that colonies were inspected weekly, yet an appendix table lists observations on dates only two days apart. Explain what this discrepancy does to the reading of the data.

answer.exemplar: The discrepancy changes how the uneven data should be read. The methods section says inspection was weekly, so a reader would treat short intervals as unusual and meaningful, perhaps as a response to a change in the colony. The appendix shows that short intervals were the normal pattern of the study, which means the spacing carries no evidential weight. Conclusions drawn from the timing of observations therefore rest on a description the evidence contradicts.

questions.explanation: The methods section sets the reader's expectation for what the data mean. When the appendix shows a different pattern of observation, that expectation misleads, and any conclusion drawn from the timing inherits the error.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader will infer from the spacing.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What supports a claim that no earlier work exists
questions.learningObjective: Explain what supports and what fails to support a negative claim
questions.stem: In a logbook, Sable claims that no one has recorded the daily flight pattern of her bees. Explain what would support that claim and what would not.

answer.exemplar: The claim requires a search that was wide enough to have found the work and a record of its extent: the catalogues and abstract indexes consulted, the keywords used, the years covered, and the names checked. Writing that there are many ways to search, or that the search found nothing, establishes nothing at all. Only a documented, wide and repeatable search can support a claim that nothing exists, and even then the claim should be hedged as no work found in the sources searched.

questions.explanation: A negative claim about the literature stands or falls on the breadth and the record of the search. An assertion that nothing was found, however sincere, carries no evidence about what was searched.
questions.hint: Ask what the search covered and can be repeated.

questions.topic: A conclusion the premises reach too far to support

answer.exemplar: The premise concerns one beekeeper, one hive and one season, and reports a single absence of brood in the supers. The conclusion asserts a general rule about how queen excluders always behave, and treats one outcome as the mechanism. The record cannot distinguish between the excluder causing the result, a queen that would not draw comb, a season that produced little honeyflow, or simple timing. A general rule needs repeated, controlled cases.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What supports a claim that no earlier work exists
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a failed search does not by itself support a negative claim
questions.stem: In a logbook, Tane writes that no previous study has counted pollen grains on bees. Explain why this claim is weak and what would improve it.

answer.exemplar: The claim is weak because it records only an unsuccessful search, and a search that failed is evidence about the search unless its extent is known. To improve it, Tane must describe the catalogues, indexes and journals consulted, the keywords and methods used, the years covered, and the people who might have done such work. Even then the claim should be worded as no work found in the sources searched, since a wider archive may exist elsewhere.

options.misconception: excuses a discrepancy by granting the summary a freedom it cannot have

options.text: That the colonies were inspected more often than the method permits
options.misconception: mistakes the number of rows for a count of inspections

questions.explanation: The appendix lists two entries for one date, which the stated method excludes. The parts of the study disagree about what was done, so the reader cannot rely on either account until the difference is explained.
questions.hint: Look for what the method forbids.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A conclusion resting on a premise nobody stated
questions.learningObjective: Identify the hidden premise and the repair a conclusion needs
questions.stem: Margit's logbook concludes: 'Because the queens I raised were imported, imported queens are not worth keeping locally.' What is the hidden premise, and what should she do about it?

options.text: The premise is that imported queens are hard to buy; she should ignore it
options.misconception: names a premise the argument does not depend on

options.text: The premise is that imported queens are cheap; she should state it openly
options.misconception: identifies a premise about price that the argument never uses

options.text: The premise is that locally raised queens are better; she should drop the conclusion
options.misconception: supplies the opposite of the premise the argument needs

options.text: The premise is that import and poor performance are related; state it and test it

questions.explanation: The conclusion treats import as the reason for the poor result, which works only if something about importing bears on performance. Naming the premise and testing it turns an assertion into a checkable claim.
questions.hint: Name the link between the cause and the effect.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A conclusion the premises reach too far to support
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a long personal record cannot establish a district rate
questions.stem: Margit's logbook states: 'I have kept bees for eleven years and never lost a colony to starvation, so starvation losses are unusual in this district.' Explain the problem with the conclusion.

answer.exemplar: The premises record eleven seasons in one apiary with one management practice, while the conclusion speaks about a district. Eleven years without a loss is evidence about that beekeeper's colonies under her own management, and it says nothing about how often managed colonies elsewhere starve, nor whether her own colonies were at risk and merely survived. The conclusion also quietly credits her method, which the record does not measure.

questions.explanation: A single long record shows what happened in one place under one practice. It cannot establish a rate for a district, and it cannot separate luck, management and season.
questions.hint: Ask what the record covers and what it claims.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a bibliographic error gives away
questions.learningObjective: Identify the bibliographic fault that reveals an unverified entry
questions.stem: Which bibliographic fault would tell a reader most that an entry in a logbook reference list was never verified?

options.text: The page range and year belong to a different work by the same author
The entry gives fewer details than the entries around it do
options.misconception: reads incompleteness as proof that the source was never opened

options.text: The journal title is abbreviated while others are written in full
options.misconception: treats a permitted abbreviation as evidence of carelessness

options.text: The entry is filed in the list under a letter it does not begin with
options.misconception: assumes a misfiling shows an unchecked entry rather than a sorting slip

questions.explanation: Details that belong to a different work can only have arrived from elsewhere. The other faults are ordinary features of a list that may or may not involve any checking at all.
questions.hint: Ask where those details could have come from.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What would substantiate a claim of contribution
questions.learningObjective: Select the addition that substantiates a comparative contribution claim
questions.stem: A logbook essay claims that its long-term hive temperature series is a contribution because it is the longest such record available. Which addition would best substantiate that claim?

options.text: A description of the logger used and how often it was read
options.misconception: describes the apparatus instead of establishing the claim

options.text: A check of published series lengths, showing this record is longer than those
An account of the seasons covered and the gaps within them
options.misconception: gives coverage information without demonstrating superiority

options.text: A statement that no other beekeeper has kept records for as long
options.misconception: reports an unsourced belief about others instead of checking

questions.explanation: The claim is comparative, so it must be settled by comparison. Checking the lengths of published series shows directly whether this record is the longest, while descriptions of equipment or coverage show nothing about that.
questions.hint: Compare with the work the claim outranks.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What supports a claim that no earlier work exists
questions.learningObjective: Choose support and wording for a negative claim about prior work
questions.stem: A logbook claims that nobody has recorded how bees respond to smoke. What would best support that claim, and how should the claim be worded?

options.text: A list of the bee books consulted, with the claim worded exactly as written
options.misconception: names a partial basis and keeps an absolute wording

options.text: A database search, with the claim worded to exclude the most recent decade
options.misconception: supplies an odd time limit and leaves the search undescribed

options.text: A documented search of the relevant indexes, worded as no work found in them
A statement that the topic is too niche to have been studied, worded generally
options.misconception: offers speculation in place of a documented search

questions.explanation: A documented search gives the claim a basis, and a qualified wording keeps it within what the search can bear. Only a claim about the sources actually searched can be defended if a reader finds a paper elsewhere.
questions.hint: Word the claim to match the search.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Limitations listed that do not touch the claim
questions.learningObjective: Identify the limitation that does not bear on a predictive claim
questions.stem: A logbook essay claims that a colony's temperament can be predicted from its lineage. Which of the following listed limitations does NOT touch that claim?

options.text: Only one person scored the temperament of each colony examined
options.misconception: removes the repeatability that the prediction needs

options.text: The colonies studied came from only four different queens
options.misconception: narrows the range of lineages on which the claim rests

options.text: The study was carried out over two separate summers
Temperament was scored late in the afternoon on every visit
options.misconception: confounds the score with a time of day rather than with lineage

questions.explanation: A limitation touches a claim when it removes something the claim needs. Scoring, number of assessors and number of lineages all bear on the prediction, but the duration of the study does not.
questions.hint: Ask which detail changes what the claim can support.
